client: I just feel so alone lately. All my friends have gone back to their normal lives after my mom died, but I'm still stuck in this grief. When they try to cheer me up or invite me out, it just makes me angry because it feels like they don't understand.
therapist:
It sounds like you're feeling deeply isolated in your grief while others seem to be moving on. The anger you feel when friends try to cheer you up suggests their support isn't landing the way they intend - would you say it feels invalidating when they respond this way?  

Your voice sounds strained as you share this - like the pain is still very raw and close to the surface. What would feel more helpful to you right now than their attempts to cheer you up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, it does feel invalidating when they try to force positivity. Like they just want me to "get over it" already because my sadness makes them uncomfortable. I don't need cheering up—I just need someone to sit with me in this pain and say "This really sucks" instead of pretending everything's fine.  

But then I feel guilty for pushing people away when they're trying to help. It's like I'm being too demanding, but their version of help just makes me feel more alone.
therapist:
It seems like you're carrying a double burden - the weight of your grief and the guilt about how you're responding to others. When you mention wanting someone to just sit with you in the pain, that strikes me as a very honest and vulnerable need.  

Let's explore this - what would it feel like to share that specific need with someone you trust? Sometimes being direct about how we want to be supported can help bridge that gap.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know if I can actually ask for that. Every time I've tried to be open about my grief, people either give me clichés or change the subject. It makes me feel even more alone, like my pain is too much for others to handle. 

The idea of being direct about needing someone to just sit with me sounds nice, but I'm scared they'll disappoint me again. What if they still don't understand?
therapist:
Your voice sounds shaky as you share this - it's clear how painful those past disappointments have been when trying to open up. That fear of being let down again makes complete sense when people haven't shown up in the ways you needed.  

It might help to think about this gradually - is there one person in your life who might be more capable of sitting with discomfort than others? Even testing the waters with small expressions of need could rebuild your trust in others' ability to support you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I get what you're saying about starting small, but honestly, even that feels risky. My brother has been more understanding than others in the past, but I'm scared if I open up and he brushes me off, it'll just confirm nobody really cares. 

The thought of reaching out makes my chest tight - like I'm setting myself up for another disappointment. Part of me wants to try, but the louder part keeps remembering all the times people seemed too busy for my problems.
therapist:
It sounds like even considering reaching out brings up a lot of anxiety - that tightness in your chest tells me this feels really vulnerable. It's understandable to feel hesitant when past attempts to connect have left you feeling dismissed.  

Let's think about this together - what would make reaching out to your brother feel slightly safer? Maybe there's a way to test the waters that feels less exposing than pouring everything out at once.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... every time I try to think of a "safe" way to reach out, my mind just goes blank. What if he doesn't respond at all? That would hurt even more than him dismissing me. At least when I don't try, I can pretend he might care.  

The idea of testing the waters makes sense, but I can already hear him sighing like I'm being dramatic again. Maybe I'm just not worth the effort to him.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between wanting connection and protecting yourself from more hurt - that's an incredibly painful place to be. The way your voice trembles as you talk about your brother suggests how much his response matters to you.  

What if we shift focus slightly - instead of figuring out if he cares, what's one small way you could care for yourself in this moment of distress?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I guess I could try to care for myself, but honestly the idea just makes me feel guilty. Like if I'm not worrying about fixing things with him, I'm being selfish. And when I've tried self-care before, it just feels empty - like putting a bandaid on a gaping wound. 

I don't know... part of me wants to believe this could help, but another part thinks "what's the point of comforting myself when the real problem is still there?" It's hard to explain.
therapist:
Your voice speeds up as you talk about self-care, and there's a tension there - like part of you wants to believe it could help, but another part feels it's not enough. That guilt you're describing is important - it sounds like you're carrying a belief that caring for yourself might mean abandoning others.  

What if we think of self-care not as a replacement for solving the bigger problem, but as a way to give yourself a bit more strength to face it? Even small acts of kindness toward yourself might help soften some of that heaviness you're carrying.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying, but I can't help feeling like self-care is just... selfish when there are so many bigger problems in the world. Like yesterday I tried to take a bath instead of answering work emails, and I just felt guilty the whole time. It's like my brain keeps saying "Who are you to relax when you could be doing something productive?"
therapist:
It sounds like even the idea of relaxing brings up a lot of guilt for you - like you're constantly measuring your worth by how much you're accomplishing. That voice saying "Who are you to relax?" seems to be really loud right now.  

Let's explore this - what would you say to a friend who was feeling guilty for taking a break? Sometimes imagining how we'd treat someone else can help us notice how harsh we're being with ourselves.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I guess if it were a friend, I'd tell them they deserve a break and that they're being too hard on themselves. But when it comes to me, it feels different. I feel like I haven't earned it yet, like I need to do more before I can allow myself to relax. It’s like there’s always something hanging over me that I should be doing instead. 

I also worry that if I start relaxing, I’ll just keep procrastinating and never get anything done. It’s hard to imagine giving myself permission without feeling like I’m letting myself off the hook.
therapist:
It's striking how much more compassion you can extend to others than to yourself - that double standard seems to be weighing heavily on you. The way your voice speeds up when talking about "earning" rest makes me wonder - what would it feel like to experiment with treating yourself with even a fraction of the kindness you'd give a friend?  

That fear of never getting anything done if you start relaxing sounds very real for you. Could we explore what a balanced approach might look like - where rest isn't the opposite of productivity, but part of sustaining it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I get what you're saying about balance, but honestly the idea of resting feels dangerous to me. Like if I give myself an inch, I'll take a mile and completely fall behind. I see friends relaxing and feel jealous, but when I try it, I just end up anxious about all the things I should be doing instead. 

It's hard to imagine rest as part of productivity when my brain keeps screaming that every minute not working is wasted time. Even when I'm exhausted, there's this voice saying I don't deserve a break until everything is perfect.
therapist:
There's real tension in your voice as you describe this - it sounds like rest feels almost threatening, as if your whole system rebels against the idea. That "screaming" voice about wasted time seems to hold a lot of power over you right now.  

What if we got curious about that voice for a moment - where do you think that belief that everything must be perfect before resting comes from? It might help to understand its roots to start changing your relationship with it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know, I guess it comes from my parents always pushing me as a kid. They'd say things like "idle hands are the devil's workshop" whenever I tried to relax. But even knowing that doesn't make the guilt go away - it feels like if I'm not productive, I'm failing somehow. 

I tried sitting still for ten minutes yesterday and ended up pacing because my brain kept listing all the things I should be doing instead. How is just "getting curious" supposed to help when the panic feels so physical?
therapist:
It makes so much sense that these beliefs feel deeply ingrained when they were reinforced for so long - your body is literally reacting as if resting is unsafe. That physical panic when you tried sitting still shows how wired this response is.  

Instead of trying to force relaxation, what if we approached this gradually? Maybe starting with just one minute of noticing your surroundings without judgment - not to relax, but simply to observe how your mind and body react in those small moments.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
